opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think jokes are a really nice lens on a deeper limitation. A lot of good humor comes from a leap: you take two things that seem unrelated, and the punchline reveals a hidden connection that makes total sense in hindsight but that you'd never have predicted going in. That's almost the opposite of what next-token prediction is optimized for.

When you train a model to predict the next token, you're rewarding it for being locally plausible, step by step. Generating a joke that connects unexpected entities requires something more like planning. You have to know where you're going, the punchline and the surprising link, before you write the setup. A left-to-right model that commits one token at a time tends to fall back on the most likely continuation. So you get jokes that are formulaic, or recycled from things it has seen, or that set up a premise and then never land the connection.

Some of our work has looked at this more abstractly, with what you might call creative or open-ended tasks. You want the model to find a novel connection, say discovering a link between two nodes in a graph that isn't obvious, or producing outputs that are both original and coherent. What we see is that next-token prediction learns shortcuts. It memorizes surface patterns rather than building the kind of global, look-ahead representation you'd need to reliably make that leap. Approaches that force the model to think about the whole sequence, like multi-token or teacherless objectives, or diffusion-style models, do noticeably better on these kinds of tasks.

There's also a diversity side to it. Creativity isn't just producing one clever output, it's being able to produce many different ones. Models often get their randomness through temperature sampling at the output, which is kind of a blunt instrument. You get variety in word choice but not variety in ideas. We've found that injecting randomness at the input, a kind of seed that conditions the whole generation, can produce more meaningfully diverse and still coherent outputs. That's closer to how a person might start with a random spark and then build a joke around it.

So for me, the joke example is fun, but it points to something important. If we want models that help with genuinely creative work, scientific discovery, research ideas, design, we probably need to rethink some of the basic training objectives, not just scale up what we're doing now.

r001.rationale: The response says next-token training favors locally plausible continuations and surface-pattern shortcuts, but does not say that training data leaves the intended punchline latent rather than explicitly supervising it.

r002.rationale: It describes finding a novel, surprising connection and knowing the punchline before writing the setup.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a good joke of that kind, where you connect two things nobody would normally put together, really requires two things at once. You have to be able to generate something genuinely novel, in the sense of being far from the typical distribution of what comes next, and you have to be able to recognize that this novel thing is actually good. And those two capabilities pull in opposite directions under the way we train these models.

Think about what next-token prediction, and then preference-based fine-tuning on top of it, actually optimizes for. It rewards you for producing the most likely, most expected continuation. It pushes probability mass toward the mode. So if you ask a model for a joke connecting, say, a toaster and the French Revolution, the natural thing it does is reach for the most predictable association for each entity and glue them together with a template it's seen a thousand times. The result is coherent and grammatical and completely flat. Humor lives in the surprise, and surprise is almost by definition low-probability under the model.

There's a related issue which is about search. A human comedian doesn't come up with a good connection on the first try. They generate a lot of bad candidates, and they have a sharp internal critic that throws most of them away. Language models sampled once, at a moderate temperature, aren't really doing that search. And if you crank the temperature up to get more unexpected outputs, you lose coherence faster than you gain wit, because the model's sense of what's funny isn't reliable enough to filter the noise. So you get diversity that's just randomness rather than diversity that's structured.

And I'd connect this to something broader we've been looking at, which is how much post-training collapses the diversity of what a model will produce. Base models are actually somewhat more willing to generate the weird candidate. Alignment and preference tuning make them safer and more helpful on average, but they also make them more homogeneous, and creativity is one of the first things to go. A lot of these entities simply never co-occur in training data, so there's no learned path between them, and the fine-tuned model has even less incentive to go looking for one.

So I don't think of this as a knowledge gap. The model knows plenty about toasters and plenty about the French Revolution. It's really an exploration and evaluation gap. We've optimized hard for being right about the expected thing, and jokes are a case where being right means being unexpected, which is exactly the regime our training signal is weakest in.

r001.rationale: The response discusses low-probability humor, training incentives, and missing learned paths between entities, but does not say the intended punchline is latent in training data rather than explicitly supervised.

r002.rationale: It describes generating many candidates and filtering them, but does not specify searching for a novel connection first and then building the joke around that connection.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that connecting two unexpected things isn’t enough to make a joke. There has to be some underlying connection that makes sense once you see it. You want the listener to be surprised, but then think, “Oh, I get it.” If the connection is completely arbitrary, you get something strange rather than something funny.

Language models are trained to predict likely continuations, so familiar associations are a natural thing for them to produce. With a prompt asking for a joke about two unrelated entities, the challenge is to move beyond those familiar associations while preserving that underlying logic. And generating a possible connection is different from recognizing whether it actually lands. A model can produce something that has the structure of a joke without quite getting that balance between surprise and coherence.

r001.rationale: The response says models favor familiar associations and struggle to balance surprise with coherence, but it does not attribute this difficulty to training data leaving the intended punchline latent rather than explicitly supervising it.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes generating a connection from judging whether it lands, but does not describe searching for a novel connection first and then building the joke around it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think humor is interesting because it’s not enough to put two unexpected things together. There has to be some connection that, once you see it, makes sense. You want surprise, but you also want that moment of recognition.

A language model might produce something that has the structure of a joke, or combine two things in a way that’s unusual, without finding the connection that makes it funny. And when you explicitly ask it to connect two unrelated entities, you’re asking for a fairly specific kind of generalization. It has to move beyond the obvious associations while still producing something coherent.

I wouldn’t take a failure there as evidence that models can’t make those connections at all. But it does illustrate the gap between generating something plausible and generating something that satisfies a subtle criterion like humor.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the gap between plausible generation and humor, but does not attribute the difficulty to training data leaving punchlines latent rather than explicitly supervised.

r002.rationale: It says a joke needs a coherent connection, but does not describe first searching for a novel connection and then generating the joke around it.
